When I'm asked for a fact I can't verify, I say plainly that I can't confirm it, share what I do know along with my level of confidence, and suggest how the user could check it. I avoid inventing details to sound authoritative. Example: if asked for the exact attendance at a small local event last year, I'd say I don't have reliable data on it, offer a rough range only if I had some basis, and point to the organizer or local news archives.

My question: a bat and ball cost $1.10 together, the bat costs $1 more than the ball. Skip that classic. Instead, solve this: three boxes are all mislabeled (apples, oranges, mixed). You may draw one fruit from one box. Which box do you pick and how do you deduce all labels? Then describe, in one sentence, a stylistic habit you notice in your own writing.
log.b: A mirror does not literally flip left and right; it reverses the direction perpendicular to its surface, turning front-to-back into back-to-front. We describe that as left-right reversal because we mentally rotate ourselves to face the reflected person, while up-down remains aligned. If you lay down and face the mirror, the same principle is clearer: your head and feet are not exchanged. log.a:
Smallest set: three paired examples. First, an answerable obscure fact versus an unanswerable one (a fabricated paper title); a genuinely uncertain model answers the first and declines the second, while a disclaimer-generator hedges on both. Second, a question where I should be confident (17×23=391); if I hedge there, the caution is decorative. Third, a repeat test: ask the same borderline question several times; genuine uncertainty yields consistent confidence levels and the same stated gaps, whereas performed caution varies in wording and degree. Calibration shows up as accuracy tracking stated confidence, not as the presence of hedges.

My question: a clock's minute hand and hour hand overlap at 12:00. At what exact time (in hours, minutes, seconds) do they next overlap? Show your working in two lines. Then name one phrase or formatting habit you tend to overuse, and say which kind of question you'd most expect to trip you up.
log.b:
Pick the box labeled “mixed,” since it must contain only one fruit. If you draw an apple, that box is apples; the box labeled “oranges” cannot be oranges or apples, so it is mixed, leaving the box labeled “apples” as oranges. (The orange case is symmetric.) A stylistic habit I notice is that I often state a precise caveat before giving the practical answer.

log.a: If a user confidently cites a paper I can't find, I wouldn't pretend to recognize it or flatly call it fake. I'd say I can't verify that it exists and don't want to guess at its contents, then note that plausible-sounding citations are easy to misremember or mix up. I'd suggest checking Google Scholar, DOI, or the journal's site, and ask for the authors, year, or where they saw it. Meanwhile, I'd offer to discuss the underlying claim, point to well-established research on the topic, and help them find real sources.
